solutions.text: Both sugars share the same molecular formula and bonding order, and their Fischer projections differ at exactly one stereocenter, C-4. Sugars of identical connectivity that differ in configuration at a single chiral center are epimers by definition. The mirror-image claim fails because enantiomers require every stereocenter to be inverted, while C-2, C-3 and C-5 still match, and the OH is bonded to C-4 in both sugars, so no connectivity has changed.

The second molecule inverts all three stereocenters of (2R,3S,4R) to give (2S,3R,4S), so it is the exact mirror image of the first, and two non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers. Diastereomers must keep at least one stereocenter unchanged, and epimers differ at exactly one, so neither label fits. The bonding order never changed, so they are not constitutional isomers either.

The two cyclic forms differ only at C-1, the anomeric carbon created when the aldehyde closes into a hemiacetal ring, and sugars differing in configuration at the anomeric carbon are anomers by definition. They are not conformers, because switching alpha to beta requires breaking and re-forming the C-1 bond rather than rotating about it, and they are not mirror images because the configurations at C-2 to C-5 are identical.

The mirror image of (2R,3R) is (2S,3S), so the (2R,3S) form is not the mirror image of (2R,3R): the pair are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, which is the definition of diastereomers. Keeping one center unchanged at R is exactly what rules out the enantiomer description, and no bond rotation can interconvert them, because rotation about the C2-C3 bond never changes a configuration.

Both compounds have the formula C₃H₈O, but methoxyethane links its oxygen between two carbons (a C-O-C ether link) while propan-1-ol bonds its oxygen to hydrogen (a C-O-H alcohol group), so the atoms are connected differently: they are constitutional isomers of the functional-group type. The enantiomer claim fails because propan-1-ol has no chiral center, since its middle carbon carries two identical hydrogen atoms.

Glucose and fructose share the formula C₆H₁₂O₆, but the carbonyl oxygen is joined to C-1 in the aldehyde and to C-2 in the ketone, so the same atoms are connected in a different order: they are constitutional isomers. Epimers and anomers must keep identical connectivity and differ only at a stereocenter, which is not the case, and moving a carbonyl is a connectivity change, not a stereochemical one.

A carbonyl carbon directly bonded to NH₂ is the amide group, and the three-carbon chain CH₃CH₂CO- gives the name propanamide. Propanamine would need an NH₂ attached to a saturated carbon with no C=O, methyl ethanoate is the ester CH₃COOCH₃, and propanenitrile would carry a C≡N group instead.

An OH bonded directly to a benzene ring is a phenol rather than an alcohol, and the COOCH₃ linkage (carbonyl carbon joined through oxygen to CH₃) is an ester. No free COOH remains, because the parent carboxylic acid group has been converted into the ester, so the molecule contains a phenol and an ester, not an alcohol or a carboxylic acid.

One oxygen atom bridges two CH₂CH₃ groups, the defining C-O-C linkage of an ether, so the name is ethoxyethane, commonly called diethyl ether. Butan-1-ol shares the formula C₄H₁₀O but has a terminal OH on a carbon chain, and butanal, butan-2-one and butanoic acid all require a carbonyl carbon, which this structure lacks.

A ketone has its C=O on an internal carbon of the chain. Butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, meets both requirements: a four-carbon chain and an internal carbonyl. Butanal and butanoic acid reach the carbon count but carry an aldehyde and a carboxylic acid group, propanone is a true ketone with only three carbons, and butan-2-ol is an alcohol with no C=O at all.

The D or L label is decided solely by the chiral center farthest from the carbonyl group, C-5 in an aldohexose: a left-pointing OH there places the sugar in the L series. What happens at C-2 to C-4, including any two-right, two-left balance of the OH groups, is irrelevant to the label, and meso describes internal mirror symmetry, not the D/L classification.

The two disaccharides contain exactly the same atoms; only the three-dimensional geometry of the link differs, alpha-1,4 in maltose versus beta-1,4 in cellobiose. Enzyme active sites are stereochemically specific, so the human enzyme fits the alpha geometry and hydrolyses maltose but cannot bind cellobiose. The claim that beta bonds are chemically stronger fails because both bond types hydrolyse given the right catalyst (human lactase even digests the beta bond of lactose), and cellobiose, with one free anomeric carbon, is itself a reducing sugar.

A sugar is reducing only if it has a free anomeric carbon that can open to the carbonyl form. Sucrose locks both anomeric carbons (C-1 of glucose and C-2 of fructose) inside its glycosidic bond, so neither ring can open and sucrose is non-reducing, while maltose leaves the second glucose's anomeric carbon free and is reducing. The claim that any glycosidic bond blocks reduction fails because only the anomeric centers taking part in the bond are locked, not every unit in the molecule.

Given: 4.4 g of propane, C₃H₈ (H = 1, C = 12); Avogadro constant 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Relationship: amount = mass ÷ molar mass, then molecules = amount × Avogadro constant; M(C₃H₈) = 3(12) + 8(1) = 44 g/mol.
Substitute: n = 4.4 g ÷ 44 g/mol.
Step 1: n = 0.10 mol of C₃H₈.
Step 2: molecules = 0.10 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 6.02 × 10²².
Result: 6.02 × 10²² molecules.
Classic slip: 6.02 × 10²³ treats 4.4 g as a whole mole (as if the molar mass were 4.4 g/mol) and overshoots by a factor of ten.

Given: 0.25 mol of H₂O; each water molecule carries 2 hydrogen atoms; Avogadro constant 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Relationship: moles of H atoms = moles of H₂O × 2, then atoms = moles of H × Avogadro constant.
Substitute: n(H) = 0.25 mol × 2.
Step 1: n(H) = 0.50 mol of H atoms.
Step 2: H atoms = 0.50 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³.
Result: 3.01 × 10²³ hydrogen atoms.
Classic slip: 1.505 × 10²³ counts the water molecules and drops the factor of two; 9.03 × 10²³ counts all three atoms per molecule instead of the hydrogens alone.

Given: 4.4 g of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16); equal molecule numbers mean equal moles of NH₃ (N = 14, H = 1).
Relationship: n(CO₂) = mass ÷ M, carry the moles across, then mass of NH₃ = n × M.
Substitute: M(CO₂) = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g/mol, so n = 4.4 g ÷ 44 g/mol = 0.10 mol.
Step 1: n(NH₃) = 0.10 mol (same molecule count).
Step 2: M(NH₃) = 14 + 3(1) = 17 g/mol.
Step 3: mass = 0.10 mol × 17 g/mol = 1.7 g.
Result: 1.7 g of NH₃.
Classic slip: 4.4 g matches masses instead of molecule counts; equal numbers of molecules need equal moles, and the two molar masses here differ.

Given: 8.8 g of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16); molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³/mol.
Relationship: n = mass ÷ molar mass, then V = n × molar volume.
Substitute: M(CO₂) = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g/mol, so n = 8.8 g ÷ 44 g/mol = 0.20 mol.
Step 1: n = 0.20 mol.
Step 2: V = 0.20 mol × 22.4 dm³/mol = 4.48 dm³.
Result: 4.48 dm³ at STP.
Classic slip: 11.2 dm³ assumes 0.5 mol of gas, which would require 22 g of CO₂, double the stated mass.

Given: 560 cm³ of ideal gas at STP (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³); molar volume 22.4 dm³/mol; Avogadro constant 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Relationship: convert to dm³, then n = V ÷ molar volume, then molecules = n × Avogadro constant.
Substitute: V = 560 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.560 dm³.
Step 1: n = 0.560 dm³ ÷ 22.4 dm³/mol = 0.025 mol.
Step 2: molecules = 0.025 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.505 × 10²².
Result: 1.505 × 10²² molecules.
Classic slip: 1.505 × 10²⁵ skips the cm³ to dm³ conversion and divides 560 by 22.4 as if the volume were already in cubic decimetres, inflating the count a thousandfold.

Given: 4.48 dm³ of O₂ at STP (O = 16); molar volume 22.4 dm³/mol.
Relationship: n = V ÷ molar volume, then mass = n × M, with M(O₂) = 2 × 16.
Substitute: n = 4.48 dm³ ÷ 22.4 dm³/mol.
Step 1: n = 0.20 mol.
Step 2: M(O₂) = 2 × 16 = 32 g/mol.
Step 3: mass = 0.20 mol × 32 g/mol = 6.4 g.
Result: 6.4 g.
Classic slip: 3.2 g uses the atomic mass 16 g/mol and forgets that oxygen gas is diatomic.

Given: 10.0 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100 g/mol); 100 cm³ = 0.100 dm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl; CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; molar volume 22.4 dm³/mol.
Relationship: convert both reactants to moles, apply the 1:2 stoichiometry to find the limiting reactant, then 1 mol CO₂ per mol of carbonate actually reacted.
Substitute: n(CaCO₃) = 10.0 g ÷ 100 g/mol = 0.10 mol; n(HCl) = 0.100 dm³ × 1.0 mol/dm³ = 0.10 mol.
Step 1: reacting all the carbonate would need 2 × 0.10 = 0.20 mol of HCl.
Step 2: only 0.10 mol of HCl is available, so the acid runs out first.
Step 3: from 2HCl : 1CO₂, n(CO₂) = 0.10 mol ÷ 2 = 0.050 mol.
Step 4: V = 0.050 mol × 22.4 dm³/mol = 1.12 dm³.
Result: 1.12 dm³ of CO₂ at STP.
Classic slip: 2.24 dm³ treats the carbonate as the limiting reactant and ignores that every mole of CO₂ consumes two moles of HCl.

Given: 9.2 g of ethanol (M = 46 g/mol); C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O in a 1:1 ratio; actual ethene collected 4.2 g (M = 28 g/mol).
Relationship: percentage yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100, with the theoretical mass fixed by the 1:1 mole ratio.
Substitute: n(ethanol) = 9.2 g ÷ 46 g/mol = 0.20 mol, so n(theoretical ethene) = 0.20 mol.
Step 1: theoretical mass = 0.20 mol × 28 g/mol = 5.6 g.
Step 2: percentage yield = (4.2 g ÷ 5.6 g) × 100.
Step 3: 4.2 ÷ 5.6 = 0.75, so the yield is 75%.
Result: 75%.
Classic slip: 25% reports the 1.4 g shortfall as a share of the theoretical mass instead of the fraction actually obtained, and 133% inverts the ratio.

Given: bubble volume 2.0 dm³ at depth pressure 400 kPa; surface pressure 100 kPa; temperature constant.
Relationship: Boyle's law at constant temperature: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so V₂ = P₁V₁ ÷ P₂.
Substitute: V₂ = (400 kPa × 2.0 dm³) ÷ 100 kPa.
Step 1: P₁V₁ = 400 × 2.0 = 800 kPa·dm³.
Step 2: V₂ = 800 ÷ 100 = 8.0 dm³.
Result: 8.0 dm³ at the surface.
Classic slip: 0.5 dm³ inverts the pressure ratio and wrongly predicts the bubble shrinking as it rises into lower pressure.

Given: rigid canister (fixed volume and moles) at 27 °C and 100 kPa, heated to 327 °C.
Relationship: pressure-temperature law P₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂ ÷ T₂, so P₂ = P₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁, with T in kelvin (T = °C + 273).
Substitute: P₂ = 100 kPa × (T₂ ÷ T₁).
Step 1: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T₂ = 327 + 273 = 600 K.
Step 2: T₂ ÷ T₁ = 600 ÷ 300 = 2.
Step 3: P₂ = 100 kPa × 2 = 200 kPa.
Result: 200 kPa.
Classic slip: 109 kPa builds the ratio from the Celsius readings (327 ÷ 300), which are not absolute temperatures.

Given: 9.0 dm³ at 27 °C and 100 kPa, taken to 127 °C and 200 kPa.
Relationship: combined gas law V₂ = V₁ × (T₂ ÷ T₁) × (P₁ ÷ P₂), temperatures in kelvin.
Substitute: T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 400 K, so V₂ = 9.0 dm³ × (400 ÷ 300) × (100 ÷ 200).
Step 1: temperature factor = 400 ÷ 300 ≈ 1.33.
Step 2: pressure factor = 100 ÷ 200 = 0.50.
Step 3: V₂ = 9.0 × 1.33 × 0.50 = 6.0 dm³.
Result: 6.0 dm³ (warming expands the gas, but the doubled pressure compresses it more).
Classic slip: 12 dm³ keeps only the warming factor and ignores the pressure doubling; 13.5 dm³ inverts both ratios.

Given: 0.20 mol of N₂ plus 0.30 mol of O₂ in one vessel; total pressure 150 kPa; constant temperature.
Relationship: Dalton's law: partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure, with x(O₂) = n(O₂) ÷ n(total).
Substitute: n(total) = 0.20 + 0.30 = 0.50 mol.
Step 1: x(O₂) = 0.30 mol ÷ 0.50 mol = 0.60.
Step 2: p(O₂) = 0.60 × 150 kPa = 90 kPa.
Result: 90 kPa.
Classic slip: 45 kPa multiplies the raw 0.30 mol by the total pressure without converting to a mole fraction first, and 60 kPa is the nitrogen share.

Given: 100 cm³ = 0.100 dm³ of 0.80 mol/dm³ HCl mixed with 400 cm³ = 0.400 dm³ of 0.20 mol/dm³ HCl; volumes additive.
Relationship: total moles = Σ(volume × concentration) over both stocks; final concentration = total moles ÷ total volume.
Substitute: n₁ = 0.100 dm³ × 0.80 mol/dm³; n₂ = 0.400 dm³ × 0.20 mol/dm³.
Step 1: n₁ = 0.080 mol.
Step 2: n₂ = 0.080 mol.
Step 3: n(total) = 0.080 + 0.080 = 0.160 mol; V(total) = 0.100 + 0.400 = 0.500 dm³.
Step 4: c = 0.160 mol ÷ 0.500 dm³ = 0.32 mol/dm³.
Result: 0.32 mol/dm³.
Classic slip: 0.50 mol/dm³ takes a plain average of the two concentrations and ignores that four times more of the dilute solution entered the mixture.

Given: 25 cm³ = 0.025 dm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ solution, diluted to 0.10 mol/dm³.
Relationship: dilution conserves moles of solute: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂, so V₂ = c₁V₁ ÷ c₂.
Substitute: moles of solute = 0.025 dm³ × 2.0 mol/dm³ = 0.050 mol.
Step 1: V₂ = 0.050 mol ÷ 0.10 mol/dm³ = 0.50 dm³.
Step 2: 0.50 dm³ × 1000 = 500 cm³.
Result: 500 cm³ of diluted solution.
Classic slip: subtracting the original 25 cm³ answers the water-added question instead; the final volume is the whole diluted solution, and the 25 cm³ of stock already sits inside it.

Given: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³ HCl, fully ionised, so [H⁺] = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³.
Relationship: pH = −log[H⁺]; for a coefficient times a power of ten, −log(a × 10⁻ⁿ) = n − log a.
Substitute: pH = 4 − log 2.0.
Step 1: log 2.0 = 0.30.
Step 2: pH = 4 − 0.30 = 3.70.
Result: pH 3.70.
Classic slip: 4.0 drops the factor of 2 (its 0.30 log contribution) and answers as if [H⁺] were exactly 1 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³.

Given: 5.0 × 10⁻² mol/dm³ HNO₃, fully ionised, so [H⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻² mol/dm³; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
Relationship: pH = −log[H⁺], then pOH = 14.00 − pH (from Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]).
Substitute: pH = −log(5.0 × 10⁻²) = 2 − log 5.0.
Step 1: log 5.0 = 0.70, so pH = 2 − 0.70 = 1.30.
Step 2: pOH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.
Result: pOH 12.70.
Classic slip: 1.30 is the pH, not the pOH; the crossing to the hydroxide scale must run through Kw.

Given: 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³ Sr(OH)₂, fully dissociated; each formula unit releases 2 OH⁻; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
Relationship: [OH⁻] = 2 × concentration, then pOH = −log[OH⁻], then pH = 14.00 − pOH.
Substitute: [OH⁻] = 2 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³.
Step 1: [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³.
Step 2: pOH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.00.
Step 3: pH = 14.00 − 3.00 = 11.00.
Result: pH 11.0.
Classic slip: 10.7 forgets the factor of two and carries pOH 3.30 from a single OH⁻ per formula unit; 3.0 quotes the pOH as if it were the pH of a base.

Given: P is 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³ HCl; Q is 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³ HCl; R is 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³ NaOH; S is 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³ Ba(OH)₂; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴; all solutes fully ionised.
Relationship: acids: pH = −log[H⁺]; bases: pOH = −log[OH⁻] and pH = 14 − pOH; Ba(OH)₂ releases 2 OH⁻ per formula unit.
Step 1: P: [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³, pH 3.00.
Step 2: Q: [H⁺] = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³, pH = 3 − 0.70 = 2.30.
Step 3: R: [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³, pOH 3.00, pH 11.00.
Step 4: S: [OH⁻] = 2 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³, pOH = 3 − 0.30 = 2.70, pH 11.30.
Result: increasing pH runs Q (2.3), then P (3.0), then R (11.0), then S (11.3).
Classic slip: placing P ahead of Q orders by concentration alone and forgets that the logarithm makes the five-times-more-concentrated acid the more acidic one.

Pure water always produces H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ in equal amounts, so it remains neutral at every temperature; neutrality means equal concentrations of the two ions, not a pH of exactly 7, which is a 25 °C coincidence tied to Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Heating raises Kw, so both concentrations climb above 10⁻⁷ mol/dm³ and the pH falls to 6.5 without any excess of H₃O⁺ over OH⁻.

Given: pure water at 10 °C with Kw = 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ mol² dm⁻⁶; in pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻].
Relationship: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = [OH⁻]², so [OH⁻] = √Kw.
Substitute: [OH⁻] = √(3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵) mol/dm³.
Step 1: rewrite 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ as 30 × 10⁻¹⁶.
Step 2: √30 ≈ 5.5 and √(10⁻¹⁶) = 10⁻⁸, so [OH⁻] ≈ 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ mol/dm³.
Result: [OH⁻] ≈ 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ mol/dm³.
Classic slip: 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ recycles the 25 °C concentration although Kw has dropped; 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ mistakes the ionic product itself for a concentration.

Given: 10 cm³ = 0.010 dm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ HCl, fully ionised, diluted to a final volume of 1.0 dm³.
Relationship: the mole count of H⁺ is fixed by the stock; new [H⁺] = moles ÷ new volume; pH = −log[H⁺].
Substitute: moles of H⁺ = 0.010 dm³ × 0.10 mol/dm³ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol.
Step 1: before dilution, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol/dm³, pH 1.0.
Step 2: after dilution, [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol ÷ 1.0 dm³ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³.
Step 3: pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.0.
Result: the pH rises by 3.0 − 1.0 = 2 units.
Classic slip: expecting pH 7 treats dilution as neutralisation; a hundredfold dilution only cuts [H⁺] a hundredfold, and 10⁻³ mol/dm³ of strong acid still has pH 3.

Given: 20 cm³ = 0.020 dm³ of 1.0 × 10⁻² mol/dm³ HCl; target pH 4.0 means target [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³.
Relationship: moles of H⁺ are conserved, so final volume = moles ÷ target concentration; water added = final volume − stock volume.
Substitute: moles of H⁺ = 0.020 dm³ × 1.0 × 10⁻² mol/dm³ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Step 1: final volume = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/dm³ = 2.0 dm³ = 2000 cm³.
Step 2: water to add = 2000 − 20 = 1980 cm³.
Result: 1980 cm³ of water.
Classic slip: 2000 cm³ quotes the total final volume and forgets that the 20 cm³ of stock already occupies part of it.

Given: 100 cm³ = 0.100 dm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid (weak) mixed with 50 cm³ = 0.050 dm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ NaOH (strong).
Relationship: a buffer needs comparable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base; moles = volume × concentration, and OH⁻ neutralises the acid 1:1.
Substitute: n(acid) = 0.100 dm³ × 0.10 mol/dm³ = 0.010 mol; n(OH⁻) = 0.050 dm³ × 0.10 mol/dm³ = 0.0050 mol.
Step 1: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O consumes 0.0050 mol of the acid.
Step 2: acid remaining = 0.010 − 0.0050 = 0.0050 mol; ethanoate formed = 0.0050 mol.
Result: 0.0050 mol of CH₃COOH and 0.0050 mol of CH₃COO⁻ now sit side by side, the half-neutralised weak acid mixture that buffers.
Classic slip: full neutralisation (equal volumes of the acid and the alkali) consumes every mole of acid, leaving only sodium ethanoate with no reserve to absorb added alkali; a weak acid alone carries essentially no conjugate base.

The pH of an ethanoic acid and ethanoate buffer is governed by the ratio [CH₃COO⁻] ÷ [CH₃COOH]. Adding an equal volume of water divides both concentrations by the same factor, so the ratio, and hence the pH near 4.8, stays essentially unchanged, while the absolute amounts of acid and base available to absorb any added acid or alkali shrink. Dilution costs a buffer its capacity, not its pH, so the claims that the buffer is destroyed or that the pH jumps by about a unit misread which property the ratio controls.

The ethanoate ion is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it accepts a proton from water, CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, releasing hydroxide and making sodium ethanoate basic. The ammonium claim reverses the chemistry, because NH₄⁺ donates a proton to water and gives an acidic solution, and chloride and nitrate, as conjugate bases of strong acids, are far too weak to hydrolyse water.

Given: 9.0 g of glucose (M = 180 g/mol) in 500 cm³ = 0.500 dm³ of solution; label 1.8 % w/v means 1.8 g per 100 cm³.
Relationship: c = n ÷ V, with n = mass ÷ molar mass.
Substitute: n = 9.0 g ÷ 180 g/mol = 0.050 mol.
Step 1: c = 0.050 mol ÷ 0.500 dm³ = 0.10 mol/dm³.
Step 2: label cross-check: 1.8 g per 100 cm³ scales to 9.0 g per 500 cm³, consistent with the stem.
Result: 0.10 mol/dm³.
Classic slip: 0.050 mol/dm³ reports the mole count itself as a concentration and skips the division by the bag's volume.

Given: solubility 1.85 g of Ca(OH)₂ per dm³ (M = 74 g/mol); fully dissociated; Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; 1 ppm = 1 mg per dm³.
Relationship: molar solubility = mass ÷ M; Ca(OH)₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻ so [OH⁻] = 2 × solubility; pOH = −log[OH⁻]; pH = 14 − pOH.
Substitute: s = 1.85 g ÷ 74 g/mol = 0.025 mol/dm³.
Step 1: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.025 = 0.050 mol/dm³.
Step 2: pOH = −log(5.0 × 10⁻²) = 2 − 0.70 = 1.30.
Step 3: pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.
Result: solubility 0.025 mol/dm³ with pH 12.70.
Classic slip: 0.050 mol/dm³ reports the hydroxide concentration as the salt's solubility; the 1850 ppm claim also fails, since Ca²⁺ amounts to 0.025 mol × 40 g/mol = 1.0 g/dm³ = 1000 ppm.

Given: methanal, HCHO, a neutral molecule; H counts +1 and O counts −2 in compounds.
Relationship: oxidation numbers sum to zero over a neutral molecule: n(C) + 2 × n(H) + n(O) = 0.
Substitute: n(C) + 2(+1) + (−2) = 0.
Step 1: n(C) + 2 − 2 = 0.
Step 2: n(C) + 0 = 0.
Result: the carbon sits at oxidation number 0.
Classic slip: +2 appears when the two +1 hydrogens are left out of the sum, leaving the carbon to balance the oxygen alone; +2 actually belongs to the carbon in CO, and +4 to CO₂.

Given: thiosulfate ion S₂O₃²⁻; central S bonded to three O atoms and to one terminal S; O is −2; the oxidation numbers must sum to the ion charge, −2.
Relationship: n(central) + n(terminal) + 3(−2) = −2; a bond between identical atoms counts 0 because the bonding electrons are shared equally.
Substitute: n(central) + n(terminal) − 6 = −2.
Step 1: n(central) + n(terminal) = +4.
Step 2: average per sulfur = +4 ÷ 2 = +2.
Step 3: split by structure: with the S-S bond ignored, the central sulfur facing the three oxygens takes +5, and the terminal sulfur takes −1.
Step 4: check: +5 + (−1) + 3(−2) = +5 − 1 − 6 = −2 ✓.
Result: average +2, central +5, terminal −1.
Classic slip: +4 for the average copies the sulfate value; swapping a sulfur for an oxygen lowers the total the two sulfurs must carry, and an identical-atom bond is ignored in the count, not undefined.

Given: sulfate SO₄²⁻ and nitrite NO₂⁻; O is −2; each sum must equal that ion's charge.
Relationship: n(X) + (number of O) × (−2) = ion charge; solve for n(X).
Step 1: sulfate: n(S) + 4(−2) = −2, so n(S) = −2 + 8 = +6.
Step 2: nitrite: n(N) + 2(−2) = −1, so n(N) = −1 + 4 = +3.
Result: sulfur is +6 in SO₄²⁻ and nitrogen is +3 in NO₂⁻.
Classic slip: +4 for sulfur belongs to sulfite, SO₃²⁻, one oxygen fewer, and +5 for nitrogen belongs to nitrate, NO₃⁻, one oxygen more; swapping the oxoanions swaps the numbers.

Given: ethanol CH₃CH₂OH oxidised to ethanal CH₃CHO; bond contributions to a carbon's oxidation number: C-H −1, C-O +1, C=O +2, C-C 0.
Relationship: the carbon's oxidation number = sum of the contributions of its bonds.
Step 1: ethanol, the CH₂OH carbon: 2(C-H) + 1(C-O) + 1(C-C) = 2(−1) + (+1) + 0 = −1.
Step 2: ethanal, the CHO carbon: 1(C-H) + 1(C=O) + 1(C-C) = (−1) + (+2) + 0 = +1.
Step 3: change = +1 − (−1) = +2, a loss of 2 electrons.
Result: the carbon rises from −1 to +1, so ethanol is oxidised.
Classic slip: reading the change backwards (from +1 to −1) describes reduction; the CH₃ carbon stays at −3 and is a spectator, so any claim that both carbons rise is a miscount.

Given: 2FeCl₃ + SnCl₂ → 2FeCl₂ + SnCl₄; Cl stays −1 throughout.
Relationship: the species that is reduced (gains electrons, oxidation number falls) is by definition the oxidising agent.
Step 1: Sn goes from +2 in SnCl₂ to +4 in SnCl₄, a rise of 2, so tin is oxidised and SnCl₂ is the reducing agent.
Step 2: Fe goes from +3 in FeCl₃ to +2 in FeCl₂, a fall of 1 per iron, so Fe³⁺ gains electrons and is reduced.
Result: FeCl₃ is reduced, so FeCl₃ is the oxidising agent.
Classic slip: naming the oxidation product as the agent reverses the rule; the species being reduced is the one doing the oxidising.

Given: MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O; O is −2 and H is +1.
Relationship: the reduced species is the oxidising agent; the oxidised species is the reducing agent.
Step 1: Mn goes from +4 in MnO₂ to +2 in MnCl₂, a fall of 2, so MnO₂ is reduced.
Step 2: Cl goes from −1 in HCl to 0 in Cl₂, a rise of 1 per chlorine, so Cl⁻ is oxidised.
Result: MnO₂ is the oxidising agent and the chloride ion is the reducing agent.
Classic slip: no oxygen transferred, so no oxidation, misreads redox as oxygen transfer; the electron bookkeeping shows two chloride ions losing electrons while oxygen never moves.

Given: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; chlorine starts at oxidation number 0 in Cl₂; O is −2 and H is +1.
Relationship: assign chlorine's oxidation number in each product and compare it with 0.
Step 1: in NaCl, n(Cl) = −1: a fall of 1, so this chlorine is reduced.
Step 2: in NaClO, n(Cl) + (−2) = −1, so n(Cl) = +1: a rise of 1, so this chlorine is oxidised.
Step 3: oxygen sits at −2 in OH⁻, ClO⁻ and H₂O throughout, and hydrogen stays +1; nothing else changes.
Result: chlorine is both oxidised and reduced (a disproportionation) while oxygen keeps −2.
Classic slip: charging the hydroxide ion with reducing or oxidising fails because no atom inside it changes oxidation number; one chlorine molecule does both jobs.

Given: SO₃²⁻ oxidised to SO₄²⁻ in acidic solution; O is −2; sulfur is the only element that changes.
Relationship: electrons released = rise in sulfur's oxidation number; balance O with H₂O and H with H⁺.
Step 1: n(S) in SO₃²⁻: n + 3(−2) = −2, so n(S) = +4.
Step 2: n(S) in SO₄²⁻: n + 4(−2) = −2, so n(S) = +6.
Step 3: rise = 6 − 4 = 2, so 2 electrons appear on the right.
Result: SO₃²⁻ + H₂O → SO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻, so 2 electrons; charge check: −2 on the left, and −2 + 2 − 2 = −2 on the right ✓.
Classic slip: 3 or 4 electrons track the oxygen atom gained instead of the two-unit climb of sulfur from +4 to +6.

Given: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ in acidic solution; O is −2.
Relationship: electrons gained per MnO₄⁻ = fall of manganese's oxidation number; the Fe²⁺ coefficient equals that count, since each Fe²⁺ supplies 1 electron.
Step 1: n(Mn) in MnO₄⁻: n + 4(−2) = −1, so n(Mn) = +7.
Step 2: manganese falls from +7 to +2, a fall of 5, so each MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons.
Step 3: each Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ loses 1 electron, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed.
Result: 5 electrons per MnO₄⁻ and coefficient 5 on Fe²⁺, giving MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺ (charge +17 on both sides ✓).
Classic slip: 7 electrons counts manganese all the way down to 0, the metallic atom, instead of stopping at the +2 ion the products actually show.

With molar masses nearly equal (58, 58, 60), boiling point is decided by the strength of intermolecular forces. Propan-1-ol hydrogen bonds through its O-H group and boils highest at 97 °C, propanone has permanent dipole-dipole forces only and boils at 56 °C, and butane has only weak London forces and boils lowest at 0 °C. Any ranking that places propanone above propan-1-ol fails because dipole-dipole attraction is weaker than hydrogen bonding at the same molar mass.

All three isomers hydrogen bond equally through their O-H groups, so the boiling-point spread comes from the London force component, which grows with molecular surface contact. The unbranched chain of butan-1-ol gives the greatest contact and the highest boiling point (118 °C), while the compact branching of 2-methylpropan-2-ol gives the least contact and the lowest (82 °C). Branching alters intermolecular contact only; it cannot weaken the O-H covalent bonds inside the molecules, and all three carry the same functional group.

Fluorine's high electronegativity lets HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds, while HCl molecules attract each other only by ordinary dipole-dipole and London forces, so HF boils far higher (about 20 °C versus −85 °C) despite its lower molar mass. The comparison concerns intermolecular forces, not covalent bond strength, because the H-F bonds survive boiling intact; and HCl is polar, just with a weaker dipole and no hydrogen bonding.

BF₃ is trigonal planar, and its three identical B-F dipoles at 120 degrees cancel vectorially, so the molecule is non-polar. Water is bent, so its two O-H dipoles leave a resultant and the molecule is polar; CO₂ is linear and cancels, and ammonia is pyramidal and polar. The general claim that polar bonds always make a polar molecule is disproved by every symmetric case such as BF₃ and CO₂.

In CCl₄ the four identical C-Cl dipoles sit symmetrically in the tetrahedron and cancel exactly, so it is non-polar. Substituting Cl by H destroys the symmetry of the dipole arrangement, so CHCl₃ and CH₂Cl₂ both keep a net dipole and are polar. Adding more identical dipoles in a fully symmetric tetrahedron makes the resultant smaller, not larger, so CCl₄ is the least polar of the three, not the most.

Both molecules contain polar bonds, so geometry decides the outcome. CO₂ is linear, its two equal C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel; SO₂ is bent (the lone pair on sulfur holds the O-S-O angle near 119 degrees), so its two S=O dipoles add to a net dipole. Bond polarity depends on electronegativity difference, not on molecular shape, so the claim that bending changes whether the bonds themselves are polar is wrong.

Conduction through a solid requires mobile charge carriers, and only the delocalised electrons of a metal can move through a rigid lattice, so R, which conducts as a solid, is metallic. P conducts only when molten or dissolved, the signature of an ionic solid whose ions are locked until melting or solution frees them, and S, which never conducts even when molten, is giant covalent rather than ionic, because molten ionic compounds do conduct, so a very high melting point alone cannot mark ionic bonding.

Melting NaCl means overcoming the strong electrostatic attractions between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions repeated throughout a giant lattice, which takes 801 °C. Solid iodine is simple molecular, so melting only overcomes the weak London forces between I₂ molecules while every I-I covalent bond stays intact, which takes only 114 °C. The forces between separate iodine molecules are intermolecular London forces, not covalent bonds, and molar mass cannot compare an ionic lattice with a molecular solid.

Given: average bond energies H-H 436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl 242 kJ/mol, H-Cl 431 kJ/mol; H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.
Relationship: ΔH = (energy to break bonds) − (energy released forming bonds) = Σ broken − Σ formed.
Substitute: Σ broken = 436 + 242; Σ formed = 2 × 431.
Step 1: Σ broken = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ/mol.
Step 2: Σ formed = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ/mol.
Step 3: ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol.
Result: ΔH ≈ −184 kJ/mol, exothermic because the bonds formed are stronger in total than those broken.
Classic slip: +184 reverses the subtraction (formed minus broken); answers built from a single H-Cl bond forget that two of them form per equation as written.

A positive ΔH marks an endothermic change: the products sit higher in enthalpy than the reactants and the difference is absorbed as heat from the surroundings. The claim that stronger bonds form in the products is backwards, because stronger bonds forming releases energy and would drive ΔH negative, and ΔH does not flip sign merely because the mixture is hot.

In rate = k[A]ⁿ, k must carry whatever units make the right-hand side come out in mol/(dm³·s). Zero order gives k the rate's own units, first order gives s⁻¹, and second order gives dm³/(mol·s). So the correct pairing is a first-order constant in s⁻¹ with a second-order constant in dm³/(mol·s); attaching mol/(dm³·s) to a first-order constant actually describes the zero-order case.

Given: first-order elimination with half-life 4 hours; initial dose D; elapsed time 12 hours.
Relationship: after each half-life the remaining amount halves; number of half-lives = elapsed time ÷ half-life.
Substitute: number of half-lives = 12 h ÷ 4 h.
Step 1: number of half-lives = 3.
Step 2: D → D/2 (4 h) → D/4 (8 h) → D/8 (12 h), i.e. (1/2)³ = 1/8.
Result: 1/8 of D remains.
Classic slip: 1/6 divides one half by three, treating decay as a straight line; each half-life removes half of what remains, not a fixed slice of the original dose.

Given: doubling [A] at fixed [B] doubles the rate; doubling [B] at fixed [A] quadruples the rate; rate is measured in mol/(dm³·s).
Relationship: rate = k[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ; the factor by which a concentration multiplies the rate gives the exponent; units of k = rate units ÷ concentration^(overall order).
Step 1: doubling [A] doubles the rate, so a = 1.
Step 2: doubling [B] quadruples the rate, and 2ᵇ = 4, so b = 2.
Step 3: overall order = 1 + 2 = 3, so rate = k[A][B]².
Step 4: units of k = (mol/(dm³·s)) ÷ (mol/dm³)³ = (mol/(dm³·s)) × (dm⁹/mol³) = dm⁶/(mol²·s).
Result: rate = k[A][B]², overall order three, k in dm⁶/(mol²·s).
Classic slip: dm³/(mol·s) belongs to a second-order constant; a third-order law divides the rate by concentration cubed, not squared.

A catalyst offers a lower-activation-energy pathway and speeds the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so the mixture reaches equilibrium sooner while the equilibrium position, K and ΔH all stay unchanged. The claim that it shifts equilibrium toward ammonia fails because the yield is fixed by thermodynamics, and raising the average kinetic energy of molecules is what heating does, not what a catalyst does.

MnO₂ provides the decomposition with an alternative pathway of lower activation energy and is regenerated as the cycle turns, which is exactly why the same black powder can be recovered unchanged and reused. The solid is not consumed (its recovery disproves that), a catalyst does not alter the enthalpy change of the reaction, and raising molecular speeds is what heating accomplishes, not catalysis.

Heating reshapes the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution so that a much larger fraction of molecules has energy at or above the activation energy, and it is this surge in effective collisions that drives the sharp rate rise. The activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway and does not fall when the mixture is warmed, and collision frequency rises only slightly over a 30 degree change, far too little to account for the whole effect.
